Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?

Search Methods A comprehensive literature search of electronic databases was conducted to identify existing, current literature regarding depression screening among college students. The following electronic databases were utilized: CINAHL, PubMed, ProQuest/Medline, ScienceDirect, Ovid, ProQuest Psychology Journals, and PsycARTICLES. Boolean search techniques were used to assist with the search methods, e.g., (depression AND college student) and (university student* OR college student* AND depressi* OR depressive symptom OR depressive disorder AND PHQ-2). Table A1 contains the literature search strategies (see Appendix A). Inclusion criteria were: (1) participants consisted of college or university students of any age; (2) studies included depression and depressive symptoms; (3) studies containing the depression screening tool called the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ); (4) studies published as peer-reviewed; (5) the setting of the studies consisted of a college, university, or primary healthcare setting; (6) studies that included depression screening via the electronic medical record (EMR). Exclusion criteria were: (1) non-college students as participants; (2) languages other than English were restricted; (3) studies before the year 2014 were restricted; (4) studies without reports of depression or depressive symptoms (5) studies whose full texts could not be found. hits.text: reviews on the PHQ-9 published to date, approxi mately 800 articles evaluated the psychometric properties of the PHQ -9 using the CTT model (4,5,8,21-29). CTT -based techniques could provide inaccurate diagnoses and do not consider the heterogeneity in each specific item (30, 31). Currently, these CCT-based methods are being complemented and, in some cases, replaced by item response theory (IRT) approaches, considered by many researchers to be the "measurement paradigm of the 21st century" (19, 32 -35). IRT -based models offer several advantages over CTT and are considered the most appropriate and robust methods for assessing the psychometric properties of screening scales such as the PHQ-9 (36,37). The idea of IRT is that test -response behavior (i.e., solving an item or choosing a specific category) can be explained by underlying person parameters (latent ability or trait) and item parameters (difficulty) (34). The relationship between the latent trait and probability of response to a given item can be expressed by different estimation models for both dichotomous and polytomous items (32,38). This approach estimates item and person parameters from the obtained data and is considered independent of the sample and test (39). In addition, IRT-based models provide a richer description of the performance of each item, greater detail on the accuracy of a measure, and when assumptions are met, scores are item - independent and invariant across different samples (33,34,40,41). Consequently, the use of IRT models may increase the validity and utility of depression screening when the PHQ-9 is used in culturally diverse settings (42,43).
